entries.note: Probably refers to the full arc of a sword's swing; first recorded in a 16th-century Protestant history, and later linked with other swinging things like bells.
An old swing idiom meaning to exert physical and social power over something; to Jess it suggests a swinging bell.
An old swing idiom with the same meaning as [[see:in one fell swoop]].
Used to explain the meaning of [[see:in a swing]].
An old swing idiom meaning to have full sway or control.
An old swing idiom meaning to have freedom of action, scope or licence.
Used as a verb to mean to be hanged; as a noun, its earliest uses refer to swinging large swords.
Probably from [[from:Charles Miner]]'s 1810 story [[from:Who'll Turn the Grindstone?]]; first meant an ulterior motive behind flattery, now usually means a grievance.
Covered in a recent episode: it comes from poor-quality homemade axes, probably from the American Civil War, whose heads would fly off.
American journalist and politician who wrote [[see:Who'll Turn the Grindstone?]] in 1810 under the pseudonym [[see:Poor Robert the Scribe]].
Miner's moral tale of a man who flatters a boy into turning a grindstone for his axe; the source of [[see:axe to grind]].
Often wrongly credited with the [[see:axe to grind]] story, which was published after his death.
Miner's pseudonym, which resembled Franklin's persona [[see:Poor Richard]] and led to the story being misattributed to Franklin.
Franklin's persona from Poor Richard's Almanac, which got mixed up with [[see:Poor Robert the Scribe]].
Means to be in jail; it refers to [[see:Sing Sing]] prison, which is up the Hudson River from New York City.
The prison was named after the [[from:Sintsink]] people, and the name roughly means stony place; it was previously Mount Pleasant State Prison.
Native American people who lived in the area for thousands of years and gave their name to [[see:Sing Sing]].
The village was renamed from Sing Sing in 1905 to distance it from the prison; the new name means something similar to [[same-root:Sintsink]].
[[see:Sing Sing]] claims this idiom for prison, probably because the prison was one big building full of prisoners.
Used of the final cable connection in telecoms and the hardest stretch of a pilgrimage; in prisons, a condemned prisoner's final walk to execution.
Did not exist before [[from:Stephen King]]'s book; it is the green linoleum walk to the electric chair in the fictional [[see:Cold Mountain Penitentiary]].
Author of the book that coined [[see:the green mile]] and was later filmed.
The fictional Louisiana prison in Stephen King's book, home of [[see:the green mile]].
Refers to slave owners punishing troublesome slaves by selling them further down the Mississippi and Ohio rivers; popularised by [[see:Uncle Tom's Cabin]].
Harriet Beecher Stowe's abolitionist novel, the best-selling American novel of the 19th century, which tied [[see:sell down the river]] to the Mississippi.
From the [[from:Sermon on the Mount]]: Jesus says to go two miles with anyone who forces you to carry their gear one Roman mile.
A Bible passage, sometimes called the antitheses, that gave several idioms, including [[gave:go the extra mile]] and [[gave:turn the other cheek]].

entries.term: an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth
entries.note: One of the idioms that come from the [[from:Sermon on the Mount]], quoted from the King James Version.
Another idiom from the [[from:Sermon on the Mount]]: if someone strikes your right cheek, offer them the other.
People who have had sex more than a mile up; the phrase took off in the 1960s, though [[see:Lord Derby]] and [[see:Lawrence Sperry]] are named as early candidates.
In 1785, Brooks's betting book recorded a wager that he would have sex with a woman in a balloon 1,000 yards up; whether he did is unknown.
London gentlemen's club, still going, whose betting book records the wager with [[see:Lord Derby]].
Inventor of the autopilot, credited as the first [[see:mile-high club]] member after he crashed in 1916 with [[see:Mrs. Waldo Polk]], though they weren't high enough.
Married socialite training for her pilot's licence who flew with [[see:Lawrence Sperry]] in 1916; they were pulled from the water naked.
Widely quoted newspaper headline about [[see:Lawrence Sperry]]'s crash; Rob couldn't find the original paper.
In 2007 it asked couples not to have sex in the double beds of its A380 suites, because the suites aren't soundproof.
Nautical, discussed in the nautical episode: a sail pressed back against the mast, halting progress; early figurative uses mention the sailing origin.
Words habitually paired even when other words would do, like [[see:pay attention]]; Jess says [[see:taken aback]] is a real idiom, not just a collocation.
Example of a [[see:collocation]]: we could just as well say [[see:give attention]].
Equally possible alternative to the [[see:collocation]] [[see:pay attention]].
Almost a fossil word, rarely used outside [[see:taken aback]] apart from forms like [[see:flung aback]].
A rarely used phrase showing that [[see:aback]] isn't quite a fossil word.
Used in Romeo and Juliet; first a horse race in which riders followed an erratic leader at set distances, like a flight of wild geese; no goose was involved.
Smoked, stinky cured herring used to lay trails for hounds; the misleading sense probably comes from [[see:William Cobbett]]'s likely made-up anecdote.
Mystery full of [[see:red herring]]s, because every suspect has a motive for killing Ratchett.
Film with major [[see:red herring]]s until Keyser Söze is revealed.
In an article, possibly from 1807, he told of using herring to draw dogs off a hare's trail, attacking the London press's false Napoleon reports ([[see:red herring]]).
The only fox hunting allowed in England and Wales: hounds hunt a laid trail rather than foxes, though they may still chase a fox they find.
The seven days either side of the winter solstice when the [[from:halcyon]] supposedly calmed the sea to nest; recorded from the 1500s, and in Shakespeare.
Not originally an adjective but a mythical Greek bird, probably the [[see:kingfisher]], said to calm the sea for 14 days while nesting.
The bird identified with the [[see:halcyon]]; its Latin name also uses the word halcyon.
French for kingfisher; one theory says it links the bird's sea-calming power to the calm weather of [[see?:St. Martin's Day]].
A spell of unusual warmth in late autumn around [[see:St. Martin's Day]]; [[see:Joan of Arc]] uses it alongside halcyon days, similar to [[see:Indian summer]].
Called Joan la Pucelle, Joan the Maiden, in Henry VI Part 1, where she says "Expect St. Martin's summer, halcyon days".
Now 11 November, and on 31 October in the old calendar, the hosts say; it gives [[see:St. Martin's summer]] its name.
Discussed before; probably named from warm spells after the first frost, first observed in Native American areas of the Mississippi valley or Appalachia, not India.
Discussed before; the season is linked to the influence of the dog star [[see:Sirius]], visible in late summer. Also called [[equivalent:canicular days]].
Another name for the [[equivalent:dog days of summer]]; canicular means doggy, related to Latin canis.
The dog star, visible in late summer, whose influence was linked to the [[see:dog days of summer]].
According to the OED, not recorded in print until a 1980s Sports Illustrated quote about [[see:Jerry Reynolds]]'s jump shot, though longer forms existed before.
[[see:Jerry Reynolds]] used this name for his jump shot, because it was good 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year.
Jerry "Ice" Reynolds, the basketball player whose remark about his jump shot is the first recorded [[see:24/7]].
A blend of [[from:malapropism]] and [[from:metaphor]] for a mix of two idioms; usually an error, but often used deliberately for humour.
Rob's [[see:malaphor]] made by combining [[see:sell down the river]] and [[see:go the extra mile]].

entries.term: we'll burn that bridge when we come to it
entries.note: The typical example of a [[see:malaphor]].
Example of an unintentional [[see:malaphor]].
Example of a [[see:malaphor]] used deliberately for humour.
Example of a [[see:malaphor]] used deliberately for humour.

entries.term: I can read him like the back of my book
entries.note: An intentionally funny [[see:malaphor]] from Giles Brandreth's wordplay book.

entries.term: the sacred cows have come home to roost with a vengeance
entries.note: A Brandreth [[see:malaphor]] that combines more than two idioms.

entries.term: talk until the cows turn blue
entries.note: Another intentionally funny [[see:malaphor]].
A dark twist on a proverb, overlapping a lot with the [[see:malaphor]].

entries.term: where there's a will, there's a lawsuit
entries.note: Example of an [[see:anti-proverb]].

entries.term: it's time to swallow the bullet
entries.note: A very dark [[see:anti-proverb]].

entries.term: easy as falling off a piece of cake
entries.note: Offered as an [[see:anti-proverb]], though Rob thinks it sounds more like a [[see:malaphor]].
Recorded from the 1830s, a century before [[see:The Seven Year Itch]], as US slang for scabies; later the urge to stray seven years into a marriage.
George Axelrod's 1952 play, filmed in 1955, which made the [[see:seven-year itch]] famous but did not coin it.
Means "and there you have it"; often linked to [[see?:Robert Gascoigne-Cecil]] promoting his nephew, but it appears only in the 1920s and probably comes from [[from?:bob]].
Prime minister and 3rd Marquess of Salisbury, who appointed his nephew [[see:Arthur Balfour]] in 1887; the doubtful Bob of [[see:Bob's your uncle]].
Appointed Chief Secretary for Ireland in 1887 by his uncle, [[see:Robert Gascoigne-Cecil]].
Slang for good from the 1700s, as in "all bob as a robin" (1721); probably behind [[gave?:Bob's your uncle]].
Listed in Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue as meaning smart, clever or spruce.
Discussed before: begging for mercy, from an Irish word for mercy that sounds like uncle, not from the English word.
From the 1766 children's story [[from:The History of Little Goody Two-Shoes]], about a poor orphan delighted at owning two shoes.
A polite Puritan American form of address for a woman, as in [[see:The Crucible]]'s "Goody Proctor".
Play quoted ("I saw Goody Proctor with the devil") to illustrate the Puritan title [[see:goody]].

entries.term: The History of Little Goody Two-Shoes
entries.note: In this 1766 story, orphan Margery Meanwell is given shoes, teaches children to read, is accused of witchcraft, and marries a rich widower; source of [[gave:goody two-shoes]].
